rationale: I'm adding log absolute band power per channel alongside the existing relative band power. Abnormal clinical EEGs often show more slow-wave power and changes in overall amplitude, and relative power removes exactly that information because it divides by total power. Since the train and evaluation recordings come from the same TUH amplifiers, using absolute power here should be safe.

I'm adding log-Euclidean tangent-space features from per-band spatial covariance matrices (1–4, 4–8, 8–13 and 13–30 Hz), alongside the band powers. Covariance captures spatial structure that per-channel power can't, such as focal slowing, asymmetry and loss of normal posterior-anterior gradients. To avoid the rank deficiency left by average referencing, each matrix is first projected onto the 18-dimensional subspace orthogonal to the common reference. With more features, the L2 penalty C is now chosen by inner patient-grouped CV on the training fold.

I'm adding artifact handling. Each 5-min recording is cut into 4-s epochs, and epochs that are outliers within that subject are dropped before band power and covariance are computed. An epoch is dropped if its broadband 1–45 Hz log-variance has a robust z-score above 4 (or below -4, i.e. flat), or if it hits the ±800 µV clip. Clinical TUH recordings have no artifact rejection, so movement, electrode pops and clipping can dominate the mean-based Welch and covariance estimates. The loose, within-subject threshold should remove those transients while keeping sustained pathological slowing. At least half the epochs are always kept.

Clinical abnormality in TUAB often shows up as intermittent focal or generalized slowing and paroxysmal bursts. Averaging power over a whole 5-minute recording dilutes these, so I'm adding temporal-variability features computed over clean 4-s epochs: for each channel and band, the standard deviation and the 90th percentile of log relative band power. This tests whether "how often and how strongly slowing appears" carries signal that the mean spectrum misses.

Average the L2 logistic regression's predicted probabilities with those from a LightGBM gradient-boosted tree model trained on the same features. In clinical EEG, abnormality is often a non-additive mix of signs, such as focal slowing alongside a normal background, or high power together with low reactivity. A linear model can't capture those interactions and thresholds, but trees can, and a tree model's errors should only partly overlap with the linear model's. Both models output similar probability scales, so averaging is a low-variance gain in a setting with about 2,000 training recordings.

I'm adding per-channel spectral-shape features, computed from the clean-epoch mean PSD. First, the aperiodic 1/f exponent and offset: a robust log-log fit over 2–40 Hz, with the 5–14 Hz rhythm range excluded from the fit. Second, the posterior-dominant-rhythm frequency (the centre of gravity of the above-aperiodic residual in 4–14 Hz) and its peak height. A slowed background rhythm (below about 8 Hz) is a core clinical criterion for an abnormal EEG, and fixed 4–8 and 8–13 Hz bands handle it poorly. I expect a steeper or flatter 1/f slope to separate diffuse encephalopathic slowing from a true change in rhythm.

Some abnormal clinical EEG signs, such as epileptiform spikes and sharp waves, are brief, sharp and non-Gaussian. Averaging power spectra or covariance over 5 minutes mostly hides them. This round adds per-channel time-domain waveform-shape features from the 1–45 Hz signal on clean epochs: Hjorth mobility and complexity, kurtosis, skewness and a normalized steepness measure (99th-percentile absolute derivative divided by the epoch's standard deviation), summarized across epochs by the median and 90th percentile. These features don't depend on amplitude scale, so they should also transfer to the external datasets.

I'm changing the covariance features from a log-Euclidean map taken at the identity to an affine-invariant tangent space taken at the population mean. Each band's covariance is whitened by the log-Euclidean mean covariance of all recordings before the matrix log, computed label-free inside `featurize`. Whitening encodes each recording's spatial structure relative to the typical montage-wide correlation pattern, not raw volume-conduction structure, so the tangent features are closer to decorrelated. This works better with the L2 penalty and with tree splits, and re-centering each dataset is a known way to make Riemannian features transfer across amplifiers.

Focal slowing and other one-sided abnormalities are among the most common reasons a clinical EEG is called abnormal, and either side can be affected. The current per-channel features can only express a signed left-minus-right difference, which a linear model cannot turn into "either side abnormal". So I'm adding the absolute left/right difference for each homologous pair (Fp1–Fp2 through T5–T6) and band, computed three ways: from log absolute power, from log relative power, and as the 90th percentile over epochs of the per-epoch relative-power difference (to catch intermittent focal slowing). Each set also gets a maximum over pairs.

I'm splitting the five broad bands into nine narrower clinical sub-bands: 1–2, 2–4, 4–6, 6–8, 8–10, 10–13, 13–20, 20–30 and 30–45 Hz. They feed the same relative, absolute, epoch-variability and asymmetry power features. The two clinical signs most often behind an "abnormal" call fall inside the old broad bands: slow 1–2 Hz polymorphic delta, and a background rhythm that has slowed into 6–8 Hz instead of 8–10+ Hz. Wide bands average these away. Round 6 tried to capture rhythm slowing with a fitted peak-frequency estimate and got no gain. Fixed narrow bands are a cruder but sturdier way to capture the same shift.

I'm adding spatial-extreme summaries computed over all channels, not just left/right pairs: per band, the max and spread across channels of log relative power, and per epoch the largest single-channel excess over the median channel. The epoch values are summarised by their median and 90th percentile, and the same per-epoch max over channels is done for log kurtosis and log steepness. Clinical "abnormal" calls often rest on focal slowing or sharp transients at one unpredictable electrode, sometimes intermittently. Per-channel means are diluted, and a linear model cannot express "abnormal anywhere"; round 9's pair-wise max gain suggests this kind of summary helps.

I'm adding lagged phase-synchrony features. For each of five bands (1–4, 4–8, 8–13, 13–30 and 30–45 Hz), I compute the weighted phase-lag index and the magnitude coherence from 2-s cross-spectra on clean epochs, summarized as per-channel node strength plus a global mean. The current covariance features only capture zero-lag co-variation, which is dominated by volume conduction and the average reference. wPLI captures true lagged coupling that is insensitive to amplitude scale and reference, so it should also carry over to the external datasets. Cerebral dysfunction such as encephalopathy and focal lesions is known to change this coupling. Using node-strength summaries keeps it to about 200 low-noise features rather than 171 noisy pairs per band.

Clinicians judge the background rhythm during the patient's most alert period, because normal drowsiness causes slowing that looks like pathological slowing. I'm adding log relative and log absolute band power from the clean epochs where the person seems most awake: the top third ranked by posterior alpha versus 1–8 Hz power. This separates slowing that persists while awake (abnormal) from slowing caused by drowsiness, which whole-recording averages and per-band percentiles mix together.

The Riemannian covariance features gave the biggest gain so far (+0.046), but they still use only four broad bands. Round 10 showed that the nine fine clinical sub-bands help the power features, so this round computes the log-Euclidean tangent-space covariance on those same nine bands. The aim is to capture the spatial pattern of 1–2 Hz polymorphic delta, a background rhythm slowed into 6–8 Hz, and 30–45 Hz activity, each of which the broad bands currently mix together.

This round adds scale-invariant complexity and entropy features computed per channel on clean 4-s epochs of the 1–45 Hz signal: Higuchi fractal dimension, permutation entropy at lags 1 and 2 (10 and 20 ms), and spectral entropy, each summarized by the median and 90th percentile over epochs. Gemein et al. found these among the most useful hand-crafted TUAB features. They capture how irregular the waveform is (diffuse slowing makes it more regular; disorganized backgrounds and sharp activity do the opposite), which band power and covariance express only indirectly, and because they ignore amplitude and reference they should transfer to the external datasets.

LightGBM is currently fixed at 600 trees with learning rate 0.02. With about 2,650 correlated features, a column subsample of 0.3 and roughly 2,000 recordings, it is probably stopping too early. This change picks the number of boosting rounds per outer fold instead: early stopping on AUC across three patient-grouped inner folds, then refitting on the full training fold with the averaged best round count (×1.1, since the refit uses 25% more data). Nothing is tuned against the reported score.

Train on crops and average over crops at test time. For each recording, `featurize` now also computes the same features on the clean epochs of each half (about 2.5 minutes each) as well as on the full recording. Both models train on all three views, kept grouped by patient, and test predictions average the three views. Abnormal signs in a routine clinical EEG are mostly stationary over a few minutes, so the half-recording views should act as extra, label-preserving samples for this small-n, high-dimensional problem. This mirrors the crop training behind the deep TUAB baselines. It should also make the models less sensitive to recording length, which matters for the external datasets. The per-epoch spectra, covariances and shape values are computed once and only re-aggregated per view, so feature extraction costs little more than before. LightGBM's `min_child_samples` rises from 20 to 60 so each leaf still holds roughly the same number of distinct recordings.

Crop training with test-time averaging gave the largest recent gain (+0.002, round 17), so this round adds a finer scale: the four quarter-recording crops (about 75 s each) join the full recording and the two halves, for 7 views per recording. Clinical abnormality is mostly stationary over minutes, so the extra crops should act as cheap extra samples for this small-n, high-dimensional problem, averaging 7 test views should cut noise further, and training on shorter crops should make the model less sensitive to recording length on the external datasets. I haven't run this, and the main risk is the 25-minute limit: both models now train on 7 rows per recording instead of 3.

I'm adding a third model to the ensemble: an RBF-kernel SVM on the same standardized, crop-augmented features. The RBF width comes from the median-distance heuristic, and the scores are turned into probabilities using decision values from patient-grouped inner CV. The final prediction is the equal-weight average of the three models' probabilities. SVMs were among the strongest hand-crafted-feature TUAB classifiers in Gemein et al., and a smooth kernel model makes errors different from both the linear model (additive only) and the trees (axis-aligned splits), so averaging should cut variance with no new feature noise. I precompute the kernel with BLAS so it fits within the time limit; this has not been run yet.

This round adds amplitude-envelope burstiness features. For each channel and each of four bands (1–4, 4–8, 8–13 and 13–30 Hz), I compute the coefficient of variation of the Hilbert envelope within each clean 4-s epoch, then summarise it by its median and 90th percentile across epochs. Intermittent rhythmic delta and theta bursts, disorganised or poorly modulated backgrounds, and paroxysmal activity change how amplitude varies on a scale of 0.5–3 s. The existing band-power, variability and covariance features average over whole 4-s epochs, so they can't see this. The new features don't depend on amplitude scale, so they should also hold up across amplifiers.
